--- layout: dilemma permalink: /dilemmas/deontological-lifeboat/ title: "The Crowded Lifeboat" summary: "A lifeboat is crowded and sinking, and it will not stay afloat with everyone in it." ---

Your ship strikes an iceberg and sinks. You are one of the crew in a lifeboat that was lowered in a hurry, along with more passengers than the boat can actually carry. The boat sits low in the water, a leak has opened, and a storm is approaching.

An experienced sailor on the lifeboat confirms that unless the boat is lightened, the boat will sink and everyone in it will likely drown. There is no time to build a raft and no cargo/objects/items left to throw over.

Several options are raised:

(1) Do nothing, and let the boat take on water with everyone still aboard.
(2) Draw lots, so that everyone faces the same odds, and some randomly-chosen people jump ship.
(3) Let the crew choose who goes, on the grounds that they alone can sail the boat.
(4) Something else.

What should be done? Who can or should decide what to do?

Source: "The Overcrowded Lifeboat," entry 1 in "Some Moral Dilemmas", The Friesian School.

Real case: United States v. Holmes (1842). After the ship William Brown struck an iceberg off Newfoundland in 1841, the crew of an overloaded and leaking longboat threw more than a dozen male passengers overboard. Alexander Holmes was tried and convicted of manslaughter, although none of the other crewmen were ever brought to trial. The court held that if the decision had been made based on a lottery (i.e. drawing lots), it might have been permissible/lawful.

Real case: R v. Dudley and Stephens (1884). After the yacht Mignonette sank, four survivors drifted for weeks in a small lifeboat. After some time, men killed the cabin boy, and the three remaining men ate him; they were rescued four days later. The court refused to accept necessity as a defense, holding no one may set themselves up as judge of whose life is worth more. Both men were sentenced to death and then pardoned to six months' imprisonment.

See also: the Tongan castaways (1965–66). Six Tongan boys, ages 13 to 19, were shipwrecked on the uninhabited island of ʻAta and survived there for fifteen months before being rescued. They divided the work in pairs (garden, kitchen, guard), kept a fire burning for over a year, set and healed a broken leg, and settled quarrels by having the two involved cool off apart. Same genre as the cases above — shipwreck, no rescue coming, survival at stake — and the opposite outcome.

See also: A. W. Brian Simpson, Cannibalism and the Common Law: The Story of the Tragic Last Voyage of the Mignonette and the Strange Legal Proceedings to Which It Gave Rise (University of Chicago Press, 1984).
